repo.name: DrillLab
repo.description: Practising until you can do it alone — four tracks that hand you less each time, ending in an empty folder and a clock

commit.message:
fix(mobile): lock the page behind the drawer, and restore it instantly (#16)

Opening the drawer on a phone left the page behind it scrollable. The scrim
stops clicks, not scrolling, so dragging over it moved the background about
88px, and closing the drawer left the page somewhere other than where it
started.

The body is now position: fixed with a negative top while the drawer is
open — not overflow: hidden, which iOS Safari ignores on body, and a phone
is where this bug lives. Three things come with it:

- Restore the position on close. While the body is fixed the document's
  scroll is 0, so without restoring it, closing snaps to the top.
- Restore it instantly. html carries scroll-behavior: smooth, so scrollTo
  animated: closing at 2055 dropped scrollY to 0 and crawled back to 2054.5
  over about 1.5 seconds. The cleanup sets documentElement's inline
  scrollBehavior to auto around the call and puts the previous inline value
  back, leaving the global rule in force everywhere else. Focus returns to
  the hamburger with preventScroll for the same reason.
- Do not restore when navigating away: a new page starts at the top. The
  sidebar's onNavigate marks "do not restore" before closing, and so does
  the [path] effect, which covers the browser Back button. Exactly one place
  marks "do restore": the moment the lock goes on.

A matching padding-right absorbs the scrollbar that disappears when a
desktop window is narrow enough to show the drawer at all.

Two probes, both verified in both directions:

  lock.mjs   4 widths x 9    wheel and scrollTo cannot move the background,
                             the drawer itself still scrolls, Escape lands
                             on the same pixel. Without the fix the
                             background goes from 374 to 1115; 12 fail.
  lock2.mjs  4 widths x 3 ways to close, 64 assertions. Samples
                             requestAnimationFrame rather than waiting for a
                             smooth scroll to settle, and asserts the
                             computed scroll-behavior really is smooth first
                             so it cannot pass vacuously. Without the fix
                             frames read 0 -> 0 -> 1 -> 4 -> 9 and 48 fail.

feat(ui): tracks vs plans, one h1 per page, and a top bar that fits 360px (#15)

Seven things that were still unclear, on top of the dial dashboard. The
design, the dials, the sidebar architecture, the alignment axes and all
content, plans, progress and routes are unchanged.

Tracks are not plans. Three different things were called "track"; now a
track is one of the five subject categories, a guided plan is one order
across Learn / Review / Practice / Code / Assess, and the drill and coding
filter is a topic. Today carries the one line that separates the first two,
under "Five categories", because that is where a first visit sees the five
cards and the sidebar's "My plan" at the same time.

/plans has one h1 per state. It used to render the picker, the catalogue
and the active dashboard at once, and the sidebar's "Change" pointed at
/plans — a link to the page you were already on. Changing now has its own
address, /plans/choose, which states that switching erases nothing.

Today is three sections. The two that went were repeats of the sidebar and
of the dials; they are one disclosure whose summary names what is inside,
including "clear progress".

The five cards say what they mean. Summaries are written by hand rather
than course blurbs cut off by -webkit-line-clamp; neither the title nor
the "pick up at" line truncates; the footer is a fixed two lines, because
it is the last grid row and its height decides where the divider sits —
two cards in one row had dividers 18px apart. At zero progress no arc is
drawn and the ring is a step thinner, its colour untouched: it is a
meaningful graphic that wants 3:1, so the quiet comes from weight. A
finished track shows a check, and its accessible name follows the
interface language.

The top bar keeps "DrillLab" at 390px. That turned out to be arithmetic:
one row has to hold 341px of controls, which measured 377 in a 360px
viewport, and every candidate for removal is spoken for. Below 520px it
wraps — brand and tools on row one, Continue across row two, where it can
show the task name again.

Also fixed: the continue line fell back to "start at the foundations,
lesson 1 of 9" whenever there was no visit record, while the card below it
said "4 / 9, pick up at lesson 5".

Validation: typecheck, lint, audit:code, build (260 pages). First Load JS
home 153, lesson 144, /plans 145, plan detail 176 — all inside budget.
Contrast 84 combinations, overflow 105, alignment axes 39, focus 558
controls driven by real Tab presses, headings across 18 routes and two
profiles, flows 176 assertions, cards 84, mobile 17 pages by 3 widths.
Zero failures.

feat(home): circular dials for the five categories

Two changes you asked for: they are categories, not courses, and the
gauges are rings rather than bars.

The ring is the better read for five cards side by side. A bar asks you to
compare five different lengths against each other; a ring shows how far
round it has gone, and it holds its own "n / N" in the middle instead of
spending a row on it. Each card also states its category — foundations,
frontend, backend, full stack — which was already in the content and had
nowhere to appear.

Three implementation details worth not undoing:

- The arc starts at twelve o'clock (rotate -90deg). Without that it starts
  at three, which reads wrong.
- Progress is stroke-dashoffset, so a change animates over --t-prog.
- A finished ring turns --ok, not the accent. The accent means "look here
  now"; a finished category is the opposite of that.

The ring's track needed its own token. It is a meaningful graphic — it is
what tells you where the total is — so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1, and
measured on a card --rule gives 1.29 and --rule-strong 1.71: at those
values you cannot see that it is a ring at all. --dial-track is 3.05:1
dark and 2.98:1 light. My first attempt dimmed --ink-4 with opacity 0.45,
which threw the computed value straight back under the line; there is a
note in the token telling the next person not to.

The parallel track spans the full row. Five cards in two columns leave the
last one alone on half a row, and it genuinely is a different kind of
thing — no prerequisites, start whenever. So the span is both layout and
meaning.

The dial numbers live in the DOM and in an aria-label; the two spans in
the middle are aria-hidden, because their text reads as "3 /9".
docs: record the dashboard home, the rail fix and the mobile scan

fix(mobile): three real defects behind "nothing is centred on my phone"

Measured every clickable control across 17 pages at 360, 390 and 414 for
four things: clipped content, escaping the viewport, claiming to centre
while padding is lopsided, and line-height bursting the box. Three were
real.

- The global :focus-visible rule set border-radius. That changes the
  geometry of the focused element, not just the ring. The search input grew
  a 6px radius the moment you focused it, nested at the top of a panel with
  a 14px radius and overflow: hidden — two radii on the same corner. Never
  put geometry in :focus-visible.
- The search placeholder carried three examples and was cut mid-word at
  360px ("…(try "filte"). The examples were always demonstrated by the six
  default results right underneath.
- In the ladder's 2x2, "Lesson exercises 148" wraps to two lines while the
  other three fit on one, so the four descriptions sat on two different
  baselines. The name now reserves two lines — with an explicit
  line-height, because inheriting the body's 1.68 makes two lines 47px
  while min-height: 2.7em is 38, leaving the wrapping cell 9px taller.

The mobile probe is now part of the suite and reports 0 across 51
page/width combinations. It has to skip the closed drawer (off-screen by
design) and anything inside a horizontal scroller — code windows and wide
tables legitimately extend past the viewport, and page-level overflow is
policed separately. Without those two exemptions it produced 167 false
positives.

fix(path): one rail, drawn once, that does not jog at the current step

The vertical line on /path has been ugly for a long time. Measured, it was
two faults stacked:

- the current step pulled its card 14px left with a negative margin and
  compensated with padding, so the text lined up but the box did not;
- the line was drawn by each step's own ::before at left: 8px, relative to
  that step's box — so the current step's segment sat at x=278 while every
  other sat at 292. The rail visibly jogged 14px exactly where the eye was
  already being drawn.

Now every step has the same padding (the current one only changes colour),
and the line is a single element on the container, so it cannot break or
shift. It carries z-index 1 to sit above the current card's fill —
otherwise the segment crossing that card is painted over and the rail
looks broken again — with the dots at 2.

No negative margins on steps. That is where this came from.

feat(home): a dashboard of tracks, and no question at the door

You asked what happens if someone today only wants to revise the question
bank. The answer was: nothing. The first screen asked "what do you want to
be ready for?" and its three answers were 42, 15 and several hours of
commitment. That intent had no entry point at all.

It was also a one-way door. That screen only rendered while `plan` was
undefined, and picking anything set it forever — so clicking the logo,
clicking Today, or typing / all failed to bring it back. You were right to
call that confusing; it was a straightforward defect.

The home page is now three bands and asks nothing:

  one line   pick up where you left off (the plan's next item if you follow one)
  five cards one per course: where you are, and the lesson you would resume
  counts     question bank, exercises, coding, arena, mocks

The chooser moved to /plans, where it is reachable whenever you want it,
with the six full cards below it behind an anchor.

Things worth not undoing:

- The home page has no filled accent block. The five cards are links, and
  the resume line is outlined with an accent edge — so /, /plans and
  /plans/[id] all cede the sidebar's Continue to the page's own actions.
- The dashboard reads a new generated content/track-manifest.ts (22 KB:
  course names, one-liners, lessons in order) instead of content/nav.ts
  (134 KB). Home's First Load JS went 178 -> 152 kB. The plan manifest
  could not be reused: it covers 65 of 80 lessons, because the interview
  course reaches plans through its questions rather than its lessons.
- Anything without a notion of "which lesson am I on" gets a count and no
  progress bar. The question bank is a queue ordered by how well you know
  each one, coding is 25 independent problems, the arena is 7 separately
  timed sittings. Drawing a percentage across those invents an order that
  does not exist.
- Course blurbs clamp to two lines. The full text is three to five lines
  because it was written for the course overview; a dashboard you cannot
  scan is not a dashboard.

feat(plans): let you run a plan again, and make switching findable

You asked whether you can change track after picking one, and said you
could not find a way to start over. Both halves were fair, for different
reasons.

**Switching existed but you could not find it.** The sidebar's "Change"
was 11px, --ink-3, thin underline — the lightest element in the column,
because I had pushed it down to obey "one dominant action per screen". My
regression asserted it was *visible*, and it passed. Visible is not the
same as findable, and only the first of those is something a script can
check. It now uses the accent text colour at 600 weight.

**Running a plan again genuinely did not exist**, and could not be built
by deleting records: plan completion is derived from lesson, exercise and
question records that plans *share* — the React plan and the complete path
both count the same nine Foundations lessons, so zeroing React by deletion
would drag the complete path down with it.

So a round is a timestamp, not a deletion. ProgressData.planRounds[planId]
marks when this round began; that plan counts only records at or after it,
every other plan still counts everything, and nothing is ever removed. To
make that possible the four completion bags now store the moment you ticked
something instead of the literal 1. No migration: 1 is smaller than any real
timestamp, so old records land on the correct side of any restart, and every
reader only ever tested truthiness.

Two things the tests caught that I had wrong:

- The round predicate was `roundStart === undefined || stamp >= roundStart`,
  which returns true when *both* are undefined — that is, a plan you have
  never restarted reported every item you have never done as done. 4/130
  rendered as 92/130 on the first run.
- A plan dropping to 0/130 looks like lost progress, so the confirmation
  states all three facts (counts from zero, ticks stay, other plans
  unaffected) and the page carries a line saying which date the round
  started, plus a way back.

Also: the fold hiding "clear progress" on the home page was labelled
"More: reference, mock scoring, sources, how progress is stored" — the one
thing you might be hunting for was the one thing the label omitted.

rounds.mjs, 13 assertions: legacy `1` values still count, restart zeroes the
plan, no record is deleted, the complete path still counts those lessons,
lesson ticks are untouched, work done after the restart counts, undo
restores. Full suite: flow 69/69, change-plan 12/12, language 49/49, focus
565 controls across 12 pages, axes 39/39, contrast 0 of 84, overflow 0 of
105, class coverage difference 0.

fix(a11y): restore visible focus on two inputs, refresh the stale baselines

Tabbing through 565 focusable controls across 12 pages found two that had
their focus ring removed:

- The search input had `outline: 0` with nothing in its place. The search
  panel has more than one focusable thing in it, so a keyboard user loses
  their place. It gets a 2px accent bottom border, and one pixel of
  padding back so the field does not jump when it takes focus.
- The sandbox editor replaced its outline with an inset ring in
  --accent-line, which is the dim olive used for hairlines. On the code
  window's near-black background that is not a focus indicator. It uses
  --accent.

Both keep `outline: 0` deliberately — one sits flush against the panel
edge and the other against a rounded window, so an outer ring is clipped.
The rule is now written down: removing the outline obliges you to supply
a replacement, in the bright accent, and the tab-through regression
enforces it.

CLAUDE.md's First Load JS baselines still quoted the numbers from before
the redesign, and its scan checklist listed three scans when there are
now eight. Both corrected, and the archived after-screenshots recaptured
— they predated the component pass by half an hour.

Note for whoever writes the next focus test: el.focus() from JavaScript
does not match :focus-visible in Chromium, so a probe built on it reports
every control that relies on the global rule as failing. Drive it with
real Tab presses.

fix(ui): reach the contract everywhere and close three regressions

- .lnext-cta restated the primary button's padding, weight, colour and
  hover on top of the class it now carries. Deleted; only its position in
  the panel and its arrow remain. The two other places that render it
  (the plan kit, the lesson plan step) now carry btn btn-primary too.
- --code-chrome-2 was scoped to .codewin/.term/.editor, but .blank-code
  hosts the same bar. Inside it the variable did not resolve, so
  `color: var(--code-chrome-2)` was invalid, color fell back to inherit,
  and in light mode the language label rendered near-black on the dark
  bar at 1.12:1. Dark mode happened to look fine, so it only showed up in
  one cell of the scan. .blank-code joins the scope and every one of the
  15 usages gains a fallback value.
- The search trigger's 44px touch rule lived in layout.css while its
  min-height lived in shell.css, which is imported later and won. It was
  32px at 430, 620 and 768px.
- Five filled buttons had var(--accent-ink) as their hover background —
  that token is the bright lime used as *text*, so hovering barely
  changed anything. They use --accent-h.
- /plans showed seven filled chartreuse actions at once, six of them the
  Start button on six equally weighted cards. Those are outlined now; the
  filled one belongs to the plan you are actually following.

Rendered font sizes across 19 pages: 23 distinct values down to 9, two of
which are em-derived from inline code.

refactor(assess): one template and one primary action for arena, mock and coding

32 hardcoded font sizes and 63 spacing literals became tokens. Two
bespoke media queries that re-set the h1 and h2 sizes on small screens
are gone — the type scale already steps down at 720px to exactly the
values they were restating.

/reference, /guide, /exams/[id] and /mock hand-rolled their page headers;
they now use the shared container and header, so they sit on the same
left axis as everything else. The same container went onto the arena and
coding detail pages. Five "lesson-meta" divs carried an inline margin-top
of 12, 14 or 16px on top of the header's own gap — three different
helpings of the same space, now none.

One filled action per page: start the timer, hand in, record the score,
open the workspace, pick a course. A real double is fixed on the arena
run page, where opening the hand-in confirmation showed both "hand in"
and "yes, hand in" filled at once — the toggle drops to outlined while
the confirmation is open, so the filled one is always the one to press.
"Mark done" on a coding page is outlined, except on the four problems
with no sandbox, where it is the only action the page has.

The sandbox mode switch was borrowing .filter-btn from the exercise
stylesheet; it is its own segmented control now, because it has an
on-state and is not a button.

refactor(lesson): normalise the code window chrome and lesson internals

71 hardcoded font sizes across code.css and lesson.css became tokens, as
did 131 spacing literals; everything left is 7px or under, which is
optical rather than layout. Seven copies of the monospace stack became
--font-mono.

The copy buttons in the code window and the terminal were two rules with
slightly different padding; they are one rule with .btn-sm geometry. They
cannot literally take .btn, because that class uses --ink and
--rule-strong, which are dark-on-dark inside a code window — the window
stays dark in both themes. Their colours come from four variables scoped
to the window instead, which only name values the file already used.

The answer-language tabs gain a permanent transparent border: the checked
rule adds one, so switching language used to jog the whole tablist by 2px.

The end-of-lesson "next lesson" link is the page's one filled action and
now carries btn btn-primary, so its height, radius and weight come from
the contract instead of being restated. "Mark as finished" drops to
outlined — it is bookkeeping, not the next step — and the recap block
loses its accent wash, which was a second chartreuse panel competing with
the CTA on the same screen.

refactor(exercise): put the six exercise types on the shared contract

47 hardcoded font sizes and 30 off-scale spacing values became tokens; two
100px pills became --r-pill. The ordering controls are real buttons now
(btn btn-sm, squared by a local width rather than by overriding the
radius, which the geometry regression checks). .opt and .filter-btn keep
their own class — one has to wrap to three lines, the other is rendered
by five components outside this scope — but they copy the button geometry
exactly, so they measure the same.

No exercise keeps a filled submit. A lesson page carries several
exercises, so one filled button each is exactly the flooding the redesign
is trying to remove; the outlined submit is still the strongest control
inside its own card, because everything around it is ghost or plain text.
The data-flow autoplay drops to outlined, and its 6x6px step dot gets a
14x18px hit area.

Two more colour reductions. .ex-level no longer changes hue by difficulty
— L1 accent, L3 warn, L4 danger is the rainbow-per-tier the tokens file
rules out, and the number already says which tier it is. .practice-focus
was a full accent wash for a notice rather than a state, so it becomes a
sunken block with a 2px accent edge.

feat(ui): one button system, eight type steps, one pill radius

An audit found 32 rules that are padded, rounded and clickable spread
across nine stylesheets, exactly one of which was .btn — so the same kind
of action appeared at three heights, four radii and two border colours
depending on which page you were on. It also found 28 hardcoded font
sizes (10, 10.5, 11, 11.5, 12, 12.5, 13, 13.5, 14, 14.5, 15, 15.5, 16,
16.5, 17, 18, 19, 26 …) and two ways of writing a pill.

.btn is now the single button system with four variants that mean 'how
heavy is this on this screen': outlined by default, one filled primary
per screen, ghost for secondary actions in a row, and a compact size.
Heights come from --h-ctl / --h-ctl-sm and rise to 44px on narrow screens
or a coarse pointer, so 'same importance, same height' holds by
construction rather than by hand.

The type scale is eight steps, --r-pill replaces 100px/999px, and
CLAUDE.md carries the contract so the next component has something to
check itself against.

docs: correct the top bar description and refresh the after screens

Two things I left inaccurate in the last commit.

The README, docs/ui-v2.md and CLAUDE.md still described the top bar as
carrying four tools including help. Help was removed from the top bar and
"How to use" moved into the sidebar next to Reference, so the top bar
carries three: search, language and theme.

The archived "after" screenshots were captured eight minutes before that
change, so they showed the old top bar — including the mobile one, which
was the whole point of the fix. Recaptured from the current build.

fix(mobile): keep the language switch visible instead of hiding it in a menu

Reported: you cannot change language on a phone. The cause was mine —
raising touch targets to 44px made the 390px top bar overflow by 38px, and
I solved that by folding language and theme into the help menu below
620px. The buttons worked, but nobody would find them: this site has a
Chinese and an English version of every sentence, so language is a switch
you reach for constantly, not a setting you configure once.

Width is reclaimed two other ways instead. The brand keeps only its mark
on narrow screens, and "How to use" moves into the sidebar next to
Reference — both are things you look up when you need them, so neither
deserves a 44px slot in the top bar. The help popover is gone entirely,
which also removes one more component language from the shell.

At 390px: menu 44 + mark 44 + Continue ~90 + search 44 + language 44 +
theme 44, plus five 8px gaps = 350 in a 358px content box.

Verified at 360, 390, 430, 620, 768, 1024 and 1440: the language button
is visible without opening anything, one tap switches, the choice is
stored, it survives a reload, the top bar does not overflow, and every
control is at least 44px on narrow screens. 49/49.

docs: record the three axes and the two sidebar primitives

Adds the measurements that motivated the change, the rule that content is
never centred, the reason the current-row bar cannot be a border-left,
and the regression each of them needs.

fix(nav): label the top bar on /guide

/guide is not in the sidebar — it lives behind the help menu — so
sectionOf returned undefined and the top bar's location line was empty
there, which looks like a rendering gap rather than a deliberate absence.

fix(plans): make changing your plan reachable from where you are

Traced from a clean browser: after picking a plan, neither the home page
nor the sidebar offered any way to change it. The only route was to think
of clicking "My plan" — which reads as "look at my plan", not "pick a
different one".

Two permanent affordances now: "Change" beside the plan name in the
sidebar, and "View the full plan / Change plan" under the Continue button
on the home dashboard.

Verified from a fresh profile at 1440 and 390: pick a plan, find the
entry on the home page, find it in the sidebar, actually switch, and
confirm no progress record is touched.

refactor(sidebar): two kinds of thing, not eight

One 252px column carried: a brand lockup, nav rows, group titles, a
bordered plan card, the Continue button, a mode eyebrow, a global
progress bar, and course rows with a lime "Start here" pill — then below
the divider, three bordered stat cells, a bordered "next up" card and two
bordered sub-mode boxes. Four kinds of border and three text axes.

There are now two: a row you can go to, and the one primary action.
.snav-item, .ctx-item, .ctx-course-top and .ctx-sub-btn share one
treatment — 34-36px tall, text at 28, and an absolutely positioned 2px
accent bar when current. The bar cannot be border-left: that shifts the
text 2px, so the current row sits off the axis the others share.

Removed along the way:
- the ✦ before parallel-track courses. The geometric display stack has
  no glyph for U+2726, so it rendered as an empty box.
- the lime "Start here" pill. The only filled thing in the sidebar is
  Continue.
- the "LEARN / REVIEW / ..." heading above each contextual section. The
  mode is already the highlighted item in the main nav.
- the global "3 / 80 lessons" bar. The plan's own 4 / 130 sits directly
  above it, and each course already shows 3 / 9.

Rows also switch from flex-wrap to grid, because a wrapping label pushed
its count onto the next line.

fix(layout): put every page on one axis instead of centring each one

Measured at 1440px, the h1 landed at 284, 326, 433 or 453 depending on
the page, while the top bar sat at 276 and the sidebar never moved. Two
causes stacked: .ui-page was centred, and each page had its own
max-width. Nothing was individually wrong, which is why it read as
"skinned" rather than "broken".

Three numbers now, in tokens.css: --gutter (content axis = sidebar width
plus this, and the top bar's padding), --rail-pad (a block's edge inside
the sidebar) and --rail-inset (a text row's edge inside a block).

Content is left-aligned, never centred; reading width is capped by each
block's own max-width. Centring is what let the axis drift with the
viewport while the chrome stayed put.

13 pages x 3 widths: top bar 284, content 284, sidebar text 28, on all
39 combinations.

UI v2: one navigation, one next action, dark high-contrast

Repositions DrillLab as a focused training command center. The sidebar is
the only navigation hierarchy and its positions are identical on every
page; the top bar carries where you are plus search, language, theme and
help. Continue exists exactly once, and the two pages whose main content
is that action hand it to the page.

A first visit asks one question with three answers instead of showing six
dense plan cards; choosing 'prepare for an assessment' is what reveals the
four assessments. With a plan active the home page becomes a dashboard:
plan, stage, progress, time left, and one card giving the next task's
type, name, estimate, position and why it is next. The plan page collapses
every stage but the current one, and shows three items inside it with the
rest behind a fold. Lesson pages drop to one content column with a
one-line position strip, and the four mode pages share one template.

Dark, high-contrast, with chartreuse reserved for current location,
progress, the single primary action and small highlights.

No lesson content, plan definition, progress semantic, URL, bilingual pair,
search coverage or assessment rule changed.

68/68 guided-plan flow assertions; 0 of 84 contrast combinations below AA;
0 of 105 overflow combinations; class coverage difference 0. First Load JS:
lesson 144 kB, home 178, /plans 141, plan detail 175 — all within budget.

a11y(plans): give the collapsed plan chip an explicit name

At 390px the chip hides the plan name and keeps only the counter, so the
link's computed accessible name was "0/130" — a screen reader user could
not tell which plan it was, or that it was a plan at all. The empty-state
chip collapsed to no name whatsoever.

Both now carry an explicit localized aria-label ("React Assessment plan,
0 of 130 completed"). The visuals are unchanged.

fix(plans): keep one continuation action when a plan is active

With a plan active the sidebar stacked two filled continuation cards on
top of each other: the guided-plan "Next" card and the ordinary Learn
"Resume" card, almost always pointing at the same lesson. Two entrances
to one destination is no entrance.

The plan panel is lazily loaded and the context sidebar renders on every
route, so the sidebar cannot compute the plan's next item itself without
dragging the manifest into the first load. lib/plan-signal.tsx inverts
it: the panel registers its next href, the Learn sidebar reads it.

  no active plan        the Resume card, unchanged
  same destination      only the plan card
  different destination a quiet secondary text link, labelled as being
                        outside the plan
  plan complete         the Resume card again, since the plan has no
                        next step left

Desktop rail and mobile drawer render the same tree, so both follow.

perf(plans): drive global plan controls from a generated lite manifest

Globally mounted plan controls (top-bar chip, sidebar panel, in-page
position strip, end-of-lesson step) used to reach content/plans, which
pulls content/nav (134 KB) plus content/nav-exercises (39 KB) to expand
a stage query into real items. That dependency in a component the root
layout mounts made webpack split nav out of the shared-by-all chunk, so
every route downloaded it again. Measured on the lesson route: First
Load JS 142 -> 195 kB (+37%).

npm run gen:nav now also emits content/plan-manifest.ts: one deduped
item table (350 rows: kind, id, examId, label, href, exercise kind,
minutes) plus per-plan stage index arrays. lib/plan-lite.ts expands it
back into objects; lib/plan-progress.ts is generic over the plan shape
so both the manifest plans and the fully resolved ones fit.

Full resolution, estimated time, per-stage rationale and the integrity
assertions stay server-side and build-time only. /plans/[planId] keeps
reading content/plans directly, since the roadmap needs all three.
Search pulls its plan entries lazily, alongside the deep index.

Lesson route First Load JS: 195 -> 144 kB (main baseline: 142 kB).

Make lessons, questions, practice, coding and the arena plan-aware

Each of these pages now says where it sits in the active plan and what
comes next, and renders nothing at all when no plan is active — free
browsing should not be interrupted by a banner.

A lesson shows its stage and item position under the header, and the end-of

next lesson demoted to a line of small text when the two differ. That step
is split into a light shell and a lazily loaded plan variant, because the
default wording is above-the-fold content that has to be server-rendered
while the plan version needs content/nav. Both render and CSS hides the
fallback once the plan version arrives; display:none elements do not
increment the CSS counter, so the numbering stays correct.

Lead the home page with the outcome question

The first screen used to ask what kind of work you wanted to do, and the
four modes answered it. That was right, but only Learn is linear: someone
who says "I am preparing for the React assessment" and opens Review finds a
bank of 105 cards and a row of filters. What they wanted was a route.

So the first question is now what you are preparing for, and six plan cards
are the answers. Someone already following a plan gets that plan instead:
its name, overall progress, current stage, the exact next item, one primary
button, and links to the full plan and to changing plans. Someone who has
turned guiding off gets the previous continue card back, plus one quiet line
pointing at /plans.

The four modes are all still there, under "Explore freely". The old
"suggested order" section is gone: a plan says the same thing far more
concretely — read these 21 lessons, then these 36 questions, then these 54
exercises — so a Learn-to-Assess arrow strip was saying it twice, vaguely.

continue.tsx keeps no plan knowledge on purpose. It ships in the shell on
every route, and resolving a plan means loading content/nav; when a plan is
active the header button is replaced by a lazily loaded plan-aware one.

Add /plans and the roadmap that is the plan's signature view

/plans asks what you are preparing for and shows six compact cards, each
with its outcome, who it is for, the stages it is made of, its scope and
its progress. /plans/[planId] is the roadmap.

The roadmap is a vertical rail of numbered stage markers. State is carried
by shape and words before colour: a finished stage is a filled marker with
a tick and a "stage complete" chip, the current one is an accent marker
with a halo and "you are here" and is the only one expanded, and later
stages are outlined and collapsed. Nothing is ever locked — every stage is
a native details element, so keyboard and screen reader behaviour comes
free and any stage opens on a click.

Items are rows when they have names worth reading — lessons, coding
problems, arena challenges, mocks — and squares when a stage holds dozens
of exercises or questions. Squares show a number when unfinished and a tick
when done, with the real title on aria-label and title, and the stage
always renders its next item as a titled row above the grid, so even a
54-square stage has one obvious target.

Plan components are loaded lazily and gated on whether a plan is active,
because they render nothing at all otherwise. plan-slots.tsx imports no
content module: it reads one field from progress and only then pulls
plan-kit in. Loading them eagerly cost /drill/[id] 152 kB and the lesson
page 155 kB of client bytes that users not following a plan would never
use. The static "Plans" entry in the header stays server-rendered so the
four modes do not shift after hydration.

Derive plan progress from the completion records that already exist

A plan stores an id and two timestamps. Nothing else. Every square in a
plan is a view of progress the user already has: lessons read lessons,
exercises read exercises (or rebuilds for the from-scratch kind), questions
read drills, coding reads coding, arena reads a passed attempt, mocks read
mocks.

This has to be derivation rather than a second ledger. Someone may rate
thirty questions on their own and pick a plan a week later; with its own
ledger the plan would show 0 / 105 and those thirty would be wasted. In the
other direction, a lesson finished inside a plan has to stay ticked in the
course. One set of facts, two views.

Two judgements worth stating. A question counts as reviewed after a single
rating, so a stage clears without forcing every card to "confident" — the
confident count is shown separately. An arena stage clears on a passed
attempt, and never locks anything: later stages stay open.

The next item is one deterministic function: first incomplete stage, then
the first incomplete item in that stage's own order, except for question
stages where the order is unseen, missed, shaky, confident. Every place
that says "next" reads that one value, so the header button, the sidebar
panel, the plan header, the roadmap highlight and the end of a lesson can
never disagree.

localStorage stays on drilllab-progress-v1. Legacy data without the three
new fields simply reads as "not following a plan".

Add a plan registry that only references existing content

Six guided plans, each an ordered sequence of stages that crosses the four
product modes: prerequisites, lessons, questions, exercises, coding
problems, rebuilds, mock. A stage is a query rather than a copy —
{from:"lessons",examId:"react"}, {from:"drills",tracks:["react"]},
{from:"coding",ids:[...]} — so titles, estimates and problem text are read
from content/nav at render time and exist in exactly one place.

The only prose a plan owns is why each stage belongs where it does. That
sentence does not exist in content/exams, because it describes the role of
a step inside a route, and a lesson only describes itself.

Mappings were taken from the real content, id by id. Where a stage has no
honest material the stage is omitted rather than padded: the Spring Boot
plan has four stages because the question bank has no Java track and there
is no Java mock. Prerequisite stages come from exam.prerequisites, which is
a relationship the content already declares.

Integrity assertions live in content/plans-assert.ts and are imported by
both prerendered plan routes, so next build reaches them: a reference to a
lesson, exercise, coding problem, arena challenge, mock, drill track,
module or course that does not exist fails the build, as does a stage that
resolves to zero items, a stage missing its why, a duplicate item inside
one plan, and a duplicate plan or stage id. They deliberately do not run
at module scope in content/plans.ts — the header carries a plan chip on
every page, and that would expand a thousand items in the browser on every
route.

The 148 exercise ids the plans need go into a separate generated file,
content/nav-exercises.ts, rather than into content/nav.ts. Folding them in
grew nav from 133 to 160 kB, which changed webpack's chunking and cost the
lesson page 145 kB it had no use for. nav.ts is now byte-identical to main.

* Let the auditor see inside escaped template literals

An agent reported that three template literals with Chinese in them could
not be translated, and worked around it by adding an English gloss comment
next to each. The cause was mine.

The code snippets are themselves written inside a template literal, so a
template literal within a snippet is escaped: \`user \${id} 不存在\`. The
backtick branch of normalize() only recognised bare backticks, so the text
inside an escaped one was compared as structure and any translation failed

because each was a real weakening rather than a syntax slip:

Blanking the whole template literal made the check pass, but it also made

So only the literal text is blanked and the interpolations are kept.

Handling escaped and bare backticks as two consecutive rules did not work
either: the \` left behind by the first rule was read as an opening
backtick by the second, which swallowed the interpolations the first rule
had deliberately preserved. One regex now handles both, with the escape
captured and required to match at the closing end.

Verified by extracting normalize() straight out of the file and running it
on the real strings: translating the text passes, changing id to uid is
caught. The three literals in iv-js2 are now properly translated. The

* Fix the audit's blind spots: it was skipping a quarter of the pairs

An agent reported that pairs written as `codeEn: SOME_CONST_EN` were never
checked, and that starterEn and templateEn were not checked at all. It was
right, and it is the worst kind of bug for a tool like this: the script
printed "✓ all pass" while quietly checking only 267 of 346 pairs. A false
assurance is worse than no script.

The extractor now covers four fields (codeEn, starterEn, templateEn,
errorOutputEn) and both ways a value can be written (an inline template
literal, or a reference to a module-level constant). Coverage went from
267 to 360.

Crucially, anything it cannot pair up is now counted and printed instead
of dropped. That silence is what let 79 pairs go unchecked.

Widening it surfaced 38 real failures, and every one was a gap in
normalize() rather than bad translation:

- The language was lost when the Chinese came from a constant, so the
  `text` exemption never applied and every method-name table with a "→ 中文"
  annotation was read as a structure mismatch.
- A multi-line JSDoc block only has /* on its first line and */ on its
  last, so the ` * text` lines in between were compared as code.
- A JSX block comment spanning lines has the same problem from both ends.
- Comments quoting a Chinese fixture ("会议" / "内容A") were reported as
  untranslated. Those strings are asserted on and must not change, so
  quoted content inside a comment no longer counts.

Two pairing bugs also came out of it. Choosing between a constant
reference and an inline literal by asking "is there a backtick nearby"
fails in both directions -- it either blocks real("text", TABLE, { codeEn:

which produced a 49-line Chinese half against a 4-line English one. It now
compares positions and takes whichever is closer. And the language regex
used exec, returning the first constructor in the window rather than the
nearest, so real("text", …) inherited the language of an earlier
real("ts", …).

string labels, JSX text, bare text in a text block, JSDoc bodies, multi-line

The seven sibling apps default to English. This one started out Chinese
only, so Chinese was the default; now that the titles, lesson bodies, code

- the server-rendered lang attribute in the layout
- the provider's initial state, which has to match the server

Align the page title with what the app actually is

The title and meta description still described the app as training for an
online assessment, which is not what it is - it is a study app built
around problems and concepts collected while learning. The README says
so; the most visible string on the site said something else.

Now: four tracks, each handing you less than the last, ending in an
empty folder and a clock. The description also names the stacks it
actually covers, including Spring Boot, which the old one left out.

Add the README

What it is, where the material comes from, and what each track hands you.

Add CLAUDE.md

Project context for future sessions: what the four tracks are, why the
question layer is derived rather than duplicated, the file ownership
rules, and the pitfalls already paid for.
Add screenshots and the local preview config

Record the information-architecture pass

Why the course archive was demoted from a main entry point to a
reference: the four tracks are the product, and 80 lessons competing
with them at the top level made the app read as a textbook.

Record why the browser runtime is CodeSandbox

What was tried, what each option could and could not do, and why 21 of
the 25 problems can run in the browser while 4 cannot - a JVM or Node
server process will not start inside an iframe, and two need fetch or
HTMLMediaElement stubbed, which the sandbox cannot intercept.

Add the routes

Five track roots plus the lesson, question, problem and sitting pages
under them. 252 pages prerendered.

Add the lesson and track components

Lesson rendering, the exercise checker, the drill session and flashcards,
the coding workspace with its editor and test panel, the arena timer, and
the progress marks that read from the shared store.

The exercise checker is regex matching after comments are stripped, not
execution - it can tell filter from push, it cannot tell whether the code
works. Every page that uses it says so.

Add the app shell and the mark

The mark is four descending bars: the four tracks, each handing you less
scaffolding than the last, down to a base that is just the arena floor.
The first three are dimmed and the fourth carries the accent - what you
are given is background, what you write yourself is the subject.

app/icon.svg is the same symbol with two constraints the component does
not have, both documented next to Mark: the leading comment has to stay
short because the metadata image loader only sniffs the first stretch of
the file for <svg>, and no comment anywhere may contain a double hyphen.

Add the content integrity checks

These run as part of the build. If a count is off, a number has a gap,
or a referenced exercise cannot be found, the build fails rather than
shipping a table that quietly disagrees with itself.

Generate the nav and search index

5 courses, 80 lessons, 148 exercises, 105 questions, 25 coding problems,
7 arena sittings.

Add the nav and search index generator

Walks every course and writes content/nav.ts plus content/search-index.ts.
Generated rather than hand-maintained because the counts are asserted at
build time, and a hand-edited index drifts within a week.

Snapshot the reference projects

The three reference projects the coding and arena problems are built
around, snapshotted so a problem page can show the exact file it is
talking about instead of pasting a copy into the lesson prose.

Regenerate with npm run gen:src after editing them.

Derive the arena track

7 timed sittings: five from-scratch rebuilds and two full mocks in a
changed scenario. An empty folder, a clock, no hints, and the answer
stays locked until you submit.

Deliberately no runtime here. Adding one would remove the hardest and
most valuable tier, so instead the local instructions have to be exact:
copyable commands, the full file tree, and real measured numbers.

Derive the coding track

25 problems: statement, explanation, and the answer behind a door you
have to open on purpose. Each carries the files, dependencies and tests
needed to attempt it.

Derive the drill track

105 short questions, each pointing back at the lesson it came from
rather than restating it. Two copies means two truths and the one you
forget to update is the one people read.

Wire the courses into a registry

exam-list.ts holds only the array, with no query functions in it. That
looks redundant next to registry.ts, and it is not: the derived tracks
need to walk every course, registry re-exports their query functions,
and ESM hoists export-from to the top of the module - so importing each
other directly produced "Cannot access EXAMS before initialization".
Pure data in its own file makes the dependency one-way.

Add the Context course

One small multi-page app whose whole point is where the Provider goes,
how one action changes two pieces of state, and what happens when the
consumers are spread across three components.

Add the mixed interview course

Seven parts: the basics people skip, two on JavaScript, two on React,
one on TypeScript, one on the back end, plus a hand-written round. This
is where the short-answer bank mostly comes from.

Add the GraphQL Federation course

Four parts across a Node subgraph and a Spring Boot service: schema and
entity resolution, resolvers and DataLoader batching, error handling and
correlation IDs, and running the two services together.

This is the course where the material stops being front-end only - the
Java side is a real Spring service, not a stub.

Add the React course

Five parts built around a note manager: state and rendering, forms and
controlled inputs, lists and identity, editing in place, and the tests
that pin the behaviour down. Ends in a from-scratch rebuild.

Add the foundations course

Starts from what npm install actually does and assumes nothing before
that. Fifteen lessons on the toolchain, modules, the JavaScript that
React needs, and the shape of a real project.

Add the client-side state layer

Theme, locale and progress, all in localStorage behind a context each.

Two notes worth keeping: the locale switch puts both languages in the
HTML and hides one with CSS, because the title and meta description are
server-rendered and cannot follow a client-side language choice. And the
progress key keeps its -v1 suffix - new fields get fallbacks in load(),
so only a change in what a field *means* needs a bump.

Define the content data model

One source of truth for every track. The types carry the invariants the
build later asserts on: a question knows which exercise it came from, a
self-authored question is flagged as such and has no source number, and
a coding problem records whether it can run in the browser.

Add the design system

A sage-and-paper palette rather than the usual blue-on-white: --paper is
an off-white with a green cast, --accent is a muted sage. Every ink and
accent value carries its measured contrast ratio against the surface it
sits on, because several were tuned to clear 4.5:1 and would otherwise
get "simplified" back under it.

One stylesheet per surface (shell, lesson, drill, coding, arena, code,
exercise, viz) on top of tokens.css and base.css.

Scaffold the Next.js project

Next 15 App Router, React 19, TypeScript strict. No CSS framework - the
styling is hand-written CSS with design tokens, so there is no Tailwind
config here.

Translate the lesson bodies across all 80 lessons (#3)

* Plumb English fields for the lesson body

The navigation reads in English now, but the lesson itself does not: the
one-line hook, the objectives, the what-the-exam-tests note, the section
headings and ledes, the common mistakes, the transfer patterns and the
recap are all Chinese-only fields.

This adds the optional English field for each and wires every render
site. No English text yet -- the plumbing has to land before the content
can be filled in per course.

objectives, recap and their English counterparts are two parallel arrays,
not one bilingual array. Alignment is by index, so a missing English
entry does not just leave a gap: from that point on every Chinese item is
paired with the wrong English one, which reads plausibly and says
something else. BilingualList therefore falls back to Chinese for the
whole list when the lengths disagree. A visibly untranslated list is far
easier to notice than a subtly misaligned one.

Three more prop types widened to ReactNode for the same reason as before,
because <T> renders two spans rather than a string: Section's title, and
LessonToc's item labels. The right-hand outline uses <T> rather than the
"中文 / English" slash format used elsewhere, since doubling the length of
every outline entry would defeat the purpose of an outline.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Wire the mock exams and the arena, and check in partial lesson-body English

Two things in one commit because they were in flight together.

Mock exams and arena problems had no English fields at all, which a
previous pass had flagged. MockExam gains English for its title, scenario,
mirrors note and per-task titles and requirements; ArenaChallenge gains
title and scenario. The seven arena scenarios are written out in full,
since that table lives in content/arena.ts rather than in a course file.

Arena titles are only partly available by design, and the type says so:
the two problems derived from mock exams pick up MockExam.titleEn, while
the four derived from from-scratch exercises stay Chinese because the
Exercise type has no English field yet. <T> falls back, so those four show
Chinese rather than breaking.

The rest is partial lesson-body content for nine files. Three agents were
translating in parallel and all three were cut off by a watchdog after
600 seconds with no tool call -- they had each been composing dozens of
long strings into a single write. The work they had finished is sound and
is checked in here rather than thrown away.

Verified before committing, per file: every Chinese value still present
byte for byte, no Chinese array changed length, and every English array
exactly as long as its Chinese counterpart. That last one matters because
alignment is by index, so a short English array silently pairs each
Chinese item with the wrong English one.

What is done in those nine files: blurb, objectives, whyForAssessment and
recap for every lesson they reached, and most section headings and
transfer rows.

What is still missing, and is the next round's job: section ledes are
almost entirely undone, a handful of headings and transfer signals, all

* Replace 16 banned idioms in the English lesson bodies

The writing standard for this app bans idioms, because the readers are
learners whose first language is not English. Sixteen had got through into
bodyEn: "blows up" / "blow up" / "blew up" eleven times, "for free" four,
"silver bullet" once.

My earlier idiom audit missed all of them, and it is worth recording why.
It scanned quoted string literals, but bodyEn is JSX -- the text sits in
element children, not in a string -- so every one of these was invisible
to it. The audit now scans lines rather than literals, and the banned list
gained the singular and past-tense forms; "blows up" was on the list from
the start but "blow up" and "blew up" were not.

Each one is replaced with what actually happens rather than a synonym:
"the last assertion fails", "it throws immediately", "fails the whole
batch", "the update does not change the original array", "scoping needs no
extra work", "it is not the right choice everywhere".

still present byte for byte.

commit.message:
Add /plans and the roadmap that is the plan's signature view

/plans asks what you are preparing for and shows six compact cards, each
with its outcome, who it is for, the stages it is made of, its scope and
its progress. /plans/[planId] is the roadmap.

The roadmap is a vertical rail of numbered stage markers. State is carried
by shape and words before colour: a finished stage is a filled marker with
a tick and a "stage complete" chip, the current one is an accent marker
with a halo and "you are here" and is the only one expanded, and later
stages are outlined and collapsed. Nothing is ever locked — every stage is
a native details element, so keyboard and screen reader behaviour comes
free and any stage opens on a click.

Items are rows when they have names worth reading — lessons, coding
problems, arena challenges, mocks — and squares when a stage holds dozens
of exercises or questions. Squares show a number when unfinished and a tick
when done, with the real title on aria-label and title, and the stage
always renders its next item as a titled row above the grid, so even a
54-square stage has one obvious target.

Plan components are loaded lazily and gated on whether a plan is active,
because they render nothing at all otherwise. plan-slots.tsx imports no
content module: it reads one field from progress and only then pulls
plan-kit in. Loading them eagerly cost /drill/[id] 152 kB and the lesson
page 155 kB of client bytes that users not following a plan would never
use. The static "Plans" entry in the header stays server-rendered so the
four modes do not shift after hydration.

commit.message:
perf(plans): drive global plan controls from a generated lite manifest

Globally mounted plan controls (top-bar chip, sidebar panel, in-page
position strip, end-of-lesson step) used to reach content/plans, which
pulls content/nav (134 KB) plus content/nav-exercises (39 KB) to expand
a stage query into real items. That dependency in a component the root
layout mounts made webpack split nav out of the shared-by-all chunk, so
every route downloaded it again. Measured on the lesson route: First
Load JS 142 -> 195 kB (+37%).

npm run gen:nav now also emits content/plan-manifest.ts: one deduped
item table (350 rows: kind, id, examId, label, href, exercise kind,
minutes) plus per-plan stage index arrays. lib/plan-lite.ts expands it
back into objects; lib/plan-progress.ts is generic over the plan shape
so both the manifest plans and the fully resolved ones fit.

Full resolution, estimated time, per-stage rationale and the integrity
assertions stay server-side and build-time only. /plans/[planId] keeps
reading content/plans directly, since the roadmap needs all three.
Search pulls its plan entries lazily, alongside the deep index.

Lesson route First Load JS: 195 -> 144 kB (main baseline: 142 kB).
The manifest chunk is now eager only on /, /plans and /plans/[planId].

commit.message:
refactor(sidebar): two kinds of thing, not eight

One 252px column carried: a brand lockup, nav rows, group titles, a
bordered plan card, the Continue button, a mode eyebrow, a global
progress bar, and course rows with a lime "Start here" pill — then below
the divider, three bordered stat cells, a bordered "next up" card and two
bordered sub-mode boxes. Four kinds of border and three text axes.

There are now two: a row you can go to, and the one primary action.
.snav-item, .ctx-item, .ctx-course-top and .ctx-sub-btn share one
treatment — 34-36px tall, text at 28, and an absolutely positioned 2px
accent bar when current. The bar cannot be border-left: that shifts the
text 2px, so the current row sits off the axis the others share.

Removed along the way:
- the ✦ before parallel-track courses. The geometric display stack has
  no glyph for U+2726, so it rendered as an empty box.
- the lime "Start here" pill. The only filled thing in the sidebar is
  Continue.
- the "LEARN / REVIEW / ..." heading above each contextual section. The
  mode is already the highlighted item in the main nav.
- the global "3 / 80 lessons" bar. The plan's own 4 / 130 sits directly
  above it, and each course already shows 3 / 9.

Rows also switch from flex-wrap to grid, because a wrapping label pushed
its count onto the next line.

fix(mobile): keep the language switch visible instead of hiding it in a menu

Reported: you cannot change language on a phone. The cause was mine —
raising touch targets to 44px made the 390px top bar overflow by 38px, and
I solved that by folding language and theme into the help menu below
620px. The buttons worked, but nobody would find them: this site has a
Chinese and an English version of every sentence, so language is a switch
you reach for constantly, not a setting you configure once.

Width is reclaimed two other ways instead. The brand keeps only its mark
on narrow screens, and "How to use" moves into the sidebar next to
Reference — both are things you look up when you need them, so neither
deserves a 44px slot in the top bar. The help popover is gone entirely,
which also removes one more component language from the shell.

At 390px: menu 44 + mark 44 + Continue ~90 + search 44 + language 44 +
theme 44, plus five 8px gaps = 350 in a 358px content box.

Verified at 360, 390, 430, 620, 768, 1024 and 1440: the language button
is visible without opening anything, one tap switches, the choice is
stored, it survives a reload, the top bar does not overflow, and every
control is at least 44px on narrow screens. 49/49.

open the workspace, pick a course. A real double is fixed on the arena
run page, where opening the hand-in confirmation showed both "hand in"

the confirmation is open, so the filled one is always the one to press.

with no sandbox, where it is the only action the page has.

The sandbox mode switch was borrowing .filter-btn from the exercise
stylesheet; it is its own segmented control now, because it has an
on-state and is not a button.

commit.message:
fix(path): one rail, drawn once, that does not jog at the current step

The vertical line on /path has been ugly for a long time. Measured, it was
two faults stacked:

- the current step pulled its card 14px left with a negative margin and
  compensated with padding, so the text lined up but the box did not;
- the line was drawn by each step's own ::before at left: 8px, relative to
  that step's box — so the current step's segment sat at x=278 while every
  other sat at 292. The rail visibly jogged 14px exactly where the eye was
  already being drawn.

Now every step has the same padding (the current one only changes colour),
and the line is a single element on the container, so it cannot break or
shift. It carries z-index 1 to sit above the current card's fill —
otherwise the segment crossing that card is painted over and the rail
looks broken again — with the dots at 2.

No negative margins on steps. That is where this came from.

fix(mobile): lock the page behind the drawer, and restore it instantly (#16)

Opening the drawer on a phone left the page behind it scrollable. The scrim
stops clicks, not scrolling, so dragging over it moved the background about
88px, and closing the drawer left the page somewhere other than where it
started.

The body is now position: fixed with a negative top while the drawer is
open — not overflow: hidden, which iOS Safari ignores on body, and a phone
is where this bug lives. Three things come with it:

- Restore the position on close. While the body is fixed the document's
  scroll is 0, so without restoring it, closing snaps to the top.
- Restore it instantly. html carries scroll-behavior: smooth, so scrollTo
  animated: closing at 2055 dropped scrollY to 0 and crawled back to 2054.5
  over about 1.5 seconds. The cleanup sets documentElement's inline
  scrollBehavior to auto around the call and puts the previous inline value
  back, leaving the global rule in force everywhere else. Focus returns to
  the hamburger with preventScroll for the same reason.
- Do not restore when navigating away: a new page starts at the top. The
  sidebar's onNavigate marks "do not restore" before closing, and so does
  the [path] effect, which covers the browser Back button. Exactly one place
  marks "do restore": the moment the lock goes on.

A matching padding-right absorbs the scrollbar that disappears when a
desktop window is narrow enough to show the drawer at all.

Two probes, both verified in both directions:

  lock.mjs   4 widths x 9    wheel and scrollTo cannot move the background,
                             the drawer itself still scrolls, Escape lands
                             on the same pixel. Without the fix the
                             background goes from 374 to 1115; 12 fail.
  lock2.mjs  4 widths x 3 ways to close, 64 assertions. Samples
                             requestAnimationFrame rather than waiting for a
                             smooth scroll to settle, and asserts the
                             computed scroll-behavior really is smooth first
                             so it cannot pass vacuously. Without the fix
                             frames read 0 -> 0 -> 1 -> 4 -> 9 and 48 fail.

 发生，焦点留在 body 上。
 
+### 【重要】抽屉打开时必须锁住背后那一页
+
+用户报的：手机上打开侧栏之后，**后面的页面照样能滚**，实测背景移了 88px；
+关掉抽屉回到原处，位置对不上，看着像跳了一下。
+蒙层（`.drawer-scrim`）只拦得住点击，拦不住滚动。
+
+锁法是把 `body` 变成 `position: fixed` 并把 `top` 设成负的滚动量，
+**不是 `overflow: hidden`** —— 后者在 iOS Safari 上对 body 不生效，
+而那正是这个站最可能被打开的地方。
+
+四件配套的事，缺一个就出新毛病：
+
+1. **解锁后要 `scrollTo` 回去。** body 固定期间文档滚动量是 0，
+   不还原的话一关抽屉就弹到页首。
+1b. **而且那一下必须是瞬间的。** `html` 上有 `scroll-behavior: smooth`
+   （styles/base.css:13），于是 `scrollTo` 变成一段动画 —— 实测在 2055 关掉抽屉，
+   scrollY 先掉到 **0**，再花约 1.5 秒滑回 2054.5。所以还原前把
+   `documentElement.style.scrollBehavior` 临时改成 `auto`，还原完把**原来的内联值**
+   放回去（原来多半是空串，直接写 `"auto"` 会永久盖掉那条全局规则）。
+   同一个理由，焦点还给汉堡时要用 **`focus({ preventScroll: true })`** ——
+   不然浏览器为了「把汉堡露出来」再滚一次，刚跳回去的位置又被滑走。
+2. **点导航走掉时不许还原。** 新页面本来就该从顶上开始。
+   所以侧栏
